title: Deepest Nesting of Picture Frames
statement:
You get a list of picture frames, where frames[i] = [w, h] is the width and height of frame i. A frame fits inside another only if it is strictly smaller in both width and height. Frames cannot be rotated.

Return the largest number of frames you can nest one inside the next, like a set of boxes within boxes.

examples.why: [1, 1] → [2, 3] → [4, 5] → [6, 7]. The [4, 6] cannot join because its width equals the width of [4, 5].
Identical frames never fit inside each other.
Only one frame of width 2 can be used. If you sort width-2 frames by rising height, a longest-increasing-heights scan would wrongly chain 2 → 3 → 4 and answer 4.

hints: If every width were different, you could sort by width and then look for the longest strictly increasing run of heights (not necessarily contiguous). Which classic problem is that?
The trouble is equal widths: two frames of the same width must never both be picked. Can you order equal-width frames so that an increasing-heights scan can pick at most one of them?

Sort by width ascending, and for equal widths by height descending. Then run the O(n log n) longest increasing subsequence on the heights: keep tails[k] = smallest height that ends a chain of length k + 1, and binary search where each height goes.

explain.intuition:
With two dimensions it looks hard, but sorting removes one of them. After sorting by width, any nesting chain appears left to right in the list, so the question becomes: what is the longest subsequence whose heights strictly increase? That is the longest increasing subsequence (LIS).

The catch is ties in width. Frames with the same width cannot nest, but sorted with rising heights they would look like a valid increasing run. Sorting equal widths by falling height fixes it: inside a group of equal widths the heights now go down, so a strictly increasing subsequence can take at most one of them. Then the standard LIS with binary search gives O(n log n): keep, for every chain length, the smallest last height seen so far, because a smaller ending leaves the most room to grow.
steps: Sort frames by width ascending; for equal widths, by height descending.
Keep an array tails, empty at first. tails[k] is the smallest height that ends a nesting chain of length k + 1.
For each height h in sorted order, binary search the first index with tails[idx] ≥ h.
If no such index exists, append h (a longer chain). Otherwise set tails[idx] = h (same length, smaller ending).
pitfalls: Sorting equal widths by ascending height. Then same-width frames chain together, as in the third example.
Using a 'first index greater than h' search. That allows equal heights in a chain, but nesting needs strictly smaller.
Running the O(n²) DP on 100 000 frames: that is 5·10⁹ steps.

solutions.title: Sort, then quadratic DP
solutions.idea: After sorting by width, best[i] is 1 plus the best chain ending at any earlier frame that is strictly smaller in both directions.

solutions.title: Sort with falling heights, then LIS by binary search
solutions.idea: Equal widths sorted by falling height cannot both join a strictly rising chain, so the answer is the LIS of the heights.

followups: Return the frames of one deepest nesting, not just its length.
Frames may now be rotated by 90 degrees. What changes?
Add a third dimension (boxes). Does the sorting trick still reduce it to one LIS?
